> **Additional Suggestion:**
> 
> Missing null-check on existingEntry before accessing existingEntry.value at line 1372-1374
> 
> View Details
> 
> 📝 Patch Details
> ### Analysis
> The code awaits a cached entry promise that could resolve to undefined (line 1245). While there's a condition checking existingEntry at line 1246, it's only for cache validation logic. The subsequent code at lines 1372-1374 attempts to call propagateCacheLifeAndTags() and access existingEntry.value.tee() without verifying existingEntry is defined.
> 
> If the promise resolves to undefined, or if workUnitStore is undefined, the code would exit the inner conditional block but continue executing lines 1372-1374, resulting in a runtime error: "Cannot read property 'value' of undefined".
> 
> The fix wraps these operations in a `if (existingEntry !== undefined)` block (new line 1367), ensuring all uses of existingEntry are protected by a proper null-check. This allows TypeScript to narrow the type from `CacheEntry | undefined` to `CacheEntry`, and prevents the runtime error when the promise resolves to undefined.

This is not accurate, `cachedEntry` can not resolve to `undefined` for the RDC.

body:
👋 If the original motivation was to address this particular edge case scenario https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/85631, which is only relevant to apps running on the Vercel platform, I suggest that we withdraw this PR for now 👀

We recently removed this long-standing Vercel platform limitation, and users should now be able to set non-ASCII characters in their response headers without 500 errors! 🎉

Regarding the mojibake recovery logic for incoming headers, I don't think Next.js should attempt to automatically decode values that may have been corrupted during transport. When a proxy is in front of the app, it is generally the user's responsibility to control how they encode non-ASCII bytes before passing them upstream, and to decode them as needed in their application code.

RFC 9110 Section 5.5 states that recipients SHOULD treat non-ASCII octets (obs-text) as opaque data:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-5.5

Applying heuristic recovery to all incoming headers risks unexpected behavior (e.g., misinterpreting intentionally-encoded values) and adds complexity that users can handle themselves when needed.

body:
Hey @wyattjoh — following up here since you mentioned in #87041 that you were experimenting with this approach.

It looks like this has been in draft with a couple of test failures since mid-January. Is this still something you're planning to land, or has the approach hit a wall?

The underlying issue (#86251) has been open for ~4 months now and has 10 upvotes — `notFound()` is essentially broken when `cacheComponents: true` is enabled with Suspense boundaries, which is a pretty common pattern. A few people in the #87041 thread have flagged it as a production blocker.

Happy to help move this forward if there's anything I can pick up — whether that's rebasing, fixing the failing tests, or iterating on the approach. Just let me know.
author: Rani367

body:
I don't have any immediate plans to pick this back up, but the approach in this PR could serve as a reasonable starting point for a proper fix. The core idea of using `controller.close()` instead of `controller.error()` for router errors so the serialized error data reaches the client is sound, though the test failures around static prerendering need to be worked through.

The buffering approach suggested in #87041 would break streaming, so that's not a viable path forward. The fix needs to preserve streaming behavior while still allowing error boundaries to handle `notFound()`/`forbidden()`/`unauthorized()` correctly within Suspense boundaries.

I may revisit this when I have some time. If anyone else wants to pick it up in the meantime, the work here should give you a head start on the direction.

body: I get the problem but now we're punishing everybody by delaying the URL. Can we come up with a middle ground that doesn't penalize Next.js apps without `basePath`?
author: eps1lon

body:
If I understand the rest of the code properly, we're printing the urls right now before the server is even up and listening. And I've been careful making sure the cli keeps responding ASAP with a first log to keep it snappy. I'm not sure I understand why you think printing those URLs right away is crucial.

Not sure if you got authoritative performance tests. Locally I'm getting a 2s timing to the server being ready and the urls being printed; feels reasonable and quick enough.

I could see an alternative where you eagerly print the result, then 2s later edit with the `basePath`. But there's 2 things that hold me back:

1. Instead of a delay, you'll get a content flash. It's not necessarily better UX.
2. For that technique to be viable, I think we'd want to rearchitect the CLI to have some control pane of what's getting logged to the screen. If we approach it really naively, we could clear and reprint the previous 4 lines. But that'll be hard to maintain (update that call site if we add another log line, or if one only shows sometime, anytime the content of the other logs change, etc.) - Doesn't feel pragmatic, and if going that route we'd talk of a larger refactor.

Open to suggestions if I miss something. But I think my proposed changes are simple and pragmatic given the context. If you have usage data available of how prevalent a `basePath` config is, it might help decide if it's an issue worth ignoring or not. I doubt it's >50% of configs, but I'd believe it's a meaningful % (likely lots of github pages.)
author: SBoudrias

body:
> I'm not sure I understand why you think printing those URLs right away is crucial.

Because it adds to the perceived performance of the dev server. The longer we wait, the slower the dev server feels like.

body:
@jwueller I'm very sorry about that. I didn't see your PR, but it looks good. I rebased it and got some value-able test, doc and performance improvements => https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/88801

I think we need to improve our workflow of handling PRs, but I don't really know how. We have >1k open PRs and github doesn't do the best job in making them discoverable...
author: sokra

body:
@sokra Thank you, I very much appreciate that! I'm happy to hear you got some mileage out of it still!

And I understand that it's hard to keep track of literally over a thousand PRs, of course. I'm honestly not sure how I'd deal with that either. Looking at those other issue keys, I'm assuming you came at it from an internal issue tracker. That probably made surfacing related work in other places harder as well.
author: jwueller

body:
Thanks for getting this over the line and huge thanks for @jwueller for the initial work. I've been waiting for this for almost 2 years now.

@sokra, how can we load files with the default/internal file/url loader that `turbopack` uses? E.g. if we have queries with `?url`, how to load them as external URLs/files? I guess I can do it with `not` perhaps.
author: kevva

body:
@kevva I've been thinking about referencing internal loaders too, but that seems like a separate problem. Maybe we could have a "spread-like" placeholder for those, that can be inserted into custom loader arrays.

As for URL loading, you can actually use this literal syntax with Turbopack, although I'm not sure if it's documented anywhere:

```ts
new URL("./asset.png", import.meta.url)
```

It gets replaced with the public URL during compile.
author: jwueller
kevva

body:
@kevva Ah right, because it avoids matching to begin with, so the defaults still apply. I guess that's a decent workaround.

Interesting that the URL literal is only documented in the context of experimental URL imports. It worked for local paths for quite a while before that already, I'm pretty sure.
author: jwueller

body: This PR also adds `type: "asset"` (https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/88788) that is slightly related.

body:
> I'm not sure if E2E is required for this kind of issue

Thanks for the feedback — good point. I initially added E2E tests to reproduce the issue in the real request flow. With the reproduction confirmed, keeping them long-term doesn’t add much value.

**After reconsidering:**

- This change is small and self-contained. (normalizing via `.toLowerCase()`)
- Adding E2E here can slow down iteration without meaningfully increasing assurance.
- The unit tests in `action-handler.test.ts` and `csrf-protection.test.ts` already exercise the modified code paths with multiple casing combinations.

I’ll remove the E2E tests and update the PR.

body:
> > The only current e2e test that uses the buildArgs option is test/e2e/react-compiler/react-compiler.test.ts, but that one is excluded from deploy tests via deploy-tests-manifest.json.
> 
> Prod tests would also be affected by this, no? I don't see `test/production/app-dir/build-output-prerender/build-output-prerender.test.ts` being ignored in deploy tests so why does it work in deploy tests or does it not actually run in deploy tests?

It's confusing. I assumed the following include pattern was ineffective, and I was just about to delete it:
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a0e2d59cf476981d18adcafa912d014664cd879a/test/deploy-tests-manifest.json#L51

because we've specified the `--type e2e` filter here:
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a0e2d59cf476981d18adcafa912d014664cd879a/.github/workflows/test_e2e_deploy_release.yml#L85

That means the deploy tests that run on canary don't include `test/production`.

However, I just found that we do add tests starting with `test/prod` here:
https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/a0e2d59cf476981d18adcafa912d014664cd879a/scripts/get-changed-tests.mjs#L63-L64

which are then used for the `Test new tests when deployed` jobs.

This discrepancy is probably not intended. @ztanner I remember you corrected me once on the question of whether production tests are deployed or not. Do you know what the intended behavior is?
author: unstubbable

body:
To unblock this PR, I've touched the two affected prod tests, and their deployment succeeded:
- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/21147806166/job/60818090278?pr=88731
- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/actions/runs/21147806166/job/60818090249?pr=88731
author: unstubbable

body:
> This discrepancy is probably not intended. @ztanner I remember you corrected me once on the question of whether production tests are deployed or not. Do you know what the intended behavior is?

@unstubbable I think the original intent was to do deploy tests for `test/production` and `test/e2e`. But a lot of `test/production` tests were testing custom `next start` specific behavior that would have failed in a deploy test. So I think we've settled on `e2e` being the one case that gets deployed, so then the mapping is:

`development` -> `next dev`
`production` -> `next start`
`integration` -> deprecated, I think this was legacy `next start`
`e2e` -> dev/start/deploy

@sokra I can't help but notice that https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/98fd3456fb19b1305816ccba8f45d43eb1e367da has been stripped of author metadata. I feel like correct attribution of my work is the least I could ask for.

Not to mention that it no longer even refers to the issues/discussions it closes, since the commit message has also been lost.
author: jwueller

body:
Hmm... I expected it to keep the author attribution of the individual commit. Maybe because it was merged by graphite...?
I initially wanted to edit your PR, but it rejected that due to permissions.
Sadly I can't modify the merge commit anymore, but I can manually add you to the release notes
author: sokra

body:
I don't know what Graphite does, but that seems like a fundamental design failure. Open source contributions are made under a specific license, and most of those _require_ attribution. Maybe it's worth evaluating that tool, if it can't even do the bare minimum correctly. Squashing commits is a destructive operation that should never happen implicitly.

I've seen this exact pattern happen in several major open source projects at this point. It also doesn't help that GitHub fails to correctly deal with git metadata in lots of places. At this point, I only trust git itself to get it right.

The permission issue could have been resolved if I had known about it, I'm sure.

Thanks for adding me to the release notes. I suppose it's something.

author: RobertAron

body:
> A fix has been merged, but not released. If you have something like pnpm/bun/patch-package it's a pretty trivial patch. Updated the nested package.json to include "sideEffects":false

Just to provide more details, the fix mentioned above is https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/commit/89ba70f2d50d33a70549bedbd5c79785810ee21b. The manual patch is to add `"sideEffects": false` to `node_modules/zod/v4/package.json` (or `v3`/`v4-mini`).

For me it doesn't seem to fix the tree-shaking problem. I used `pnpm` patch and ran `next experimental-analyze`, still seeing all the locales being bundled on the server side. I don't have reference to any of the locales in my code, and by default `en` is loaded automatically (for `zod`)

body:
Thanks for coming back!

The reasoning for relative paths makes sense, a couple of clarifying questions:

1. For bare specifiers like `test-pkg/foo` going to `test-pkg/foo/alt`, is project-root resolution also intentional? In this case, Node's resolution algorithm would naturally find the package from wherever it's imported, so resolving from project root seems to change that behavior in a way that breaks transitive deps.
2. The webpack config equivalent works for transitive dependencies as far as I can see, is that difference in behavior intentional, or should Turbopack match webpack here?

I am not super familiar with Turbopack and am trying to put in some PRs to get more familiar and spelunk around the codebase, so it's possible that I am missing some historical context here :-)

That would allow compaction that handle that differently. And we would also detect that case during lookup. This would also handle the delete case, where Delete + Multiple has value bytes and only that key value pair is deleted.

body:
> What makes module evaluation different from other frames to be special cased?

When an error happens during module evaluation (importing node_modules code), you need to know in which package it happened (and that import path to it). Pointing to user code (maybe a page module that imports whatever library) isn't very useful in that case.

On the other hand, errors that are outside of module evaluation, they are caused by a call to that library code in user code and we can point to that line. That would be useful in most cases, so the ignore-listing makes sense here.

body:
@naaa760 I tried re-running the tests a few times in CI (a lot of them are just flaky), but I think this change might be breaking something. A lot of the tests are failing with errors like:

```
FetchError: request to http://localhost:35445/api/test failed, reason: socket hang up
```
author: bgw

body:
@bgw 
sir the failures were from listening to req.close (it runs when the request body is read) and i have switched to only req.aborted, so we only clean up on client abort. 
That should fix the socket hang up and keep the zlib leak fix.
please let me know!

> Do we send deprecated warning (from `config.ts`) for users using the option? Kinda subtle breaking change might be better to indicate on CLI along side the deprecated JSDoc you added

I don't think this is a breaking change, otherwise all the experimental flag is breaking change. We didn't really change the default value or rename the flag either. body:
> You're absolutely right

@jaffarkeikei I appreciate the contribution you made with https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/89127, but I highly recommend that you do not use LLMs to write responses to GitHub issues or pull requests to projects where you do not already have an established reputation. It's also good practice to be clear and transparent about what portions of the work you used LLMs for, to help the reviewer understand where to focus their attention.

I don't mean this to say that you shouldn't use LLMs. You should use them. They're an incredible tool, but you need to be cautious in how you use them in the context of third-party open source contributions.

You may have seen that [many large open source projects have stopped accepting community pull requests because of an increasing level of spam](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46641042). Heavily relying on an LLM as a community contributor can come off as "low effort". I know this isn't the case here, based on your other contributions, but it can easily come off wrong.

Reviewing community PRs often requires a lot more effort on an open source maintainer's time than most other work, because until a contributor is trusted, it requires significantly more scrutiny. That's either because of a higher risk of honest mistakes from somebody unfamiliar with the code, or concerns about [supply chain attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XZ_Utils_backdoor). A lot of times, we review PRs not because of the bugs they may fix, but because we want to help others grow, and an LLM generated response hurts that trust.

I understand that you're a student, and if you're looking to learn, contributing to open source can be valuable. I benefited and learned a lot from contributing to similar projects myself. I love reviewing changes from new contributors.

However, there's a balance here. If you're making contributions to game some metrics on GitHub, that's not a good use of anyone's time. Open source is often most rewarding when you've personally encountered real issues using a project, and you're building the solution out of that experience.

I hope this doesn't turn you off to contributing to Next.js. I'd love to see more of your PRs here. Just link your PRs to clear issues or reproductions, and be clear and transparent about what you do or don't understand, and how you used LLMs to help fill that knowledge gap.

body:
We reverted this in https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/89283

This was missing the deserialization part which has security (DoS) implications: Deserializing BigInts needs to be limited since unreasonably large numbers (500+ digits) take a lot of blocking CPU time (upwards of 50ms).

If people really want to put BigInt into their search params, they can call .toString themselves and deserialize it. But since this makes a DDoS pretty trivial, we don't want to encourage BigInt for search params unless Next.js can make deserialization safe.

body:
Thanks for checking, @icyJoseph! I've done extensive testing on my main production app (where I first discovered the issue), and because it didn’t appear in minimal setups, I copied over the exact dependency versions. That allowed me to reproduce the bug reliably.

I’ve created a minimal reproduction here:  
https://github.com/andreibalan-dev/nextjs-webpack-issue-repro

## Steps to reproduce
```bash
git clone https://github.com/andreibalan-dev/nextjs-webpack-issue-repro.git
cd nextjs-webpack-issue-repro
npm ci                    # IMPORTANT: must use npm ci for exact lockfile versions
npm run build:webpack
```

## Verifying dev-only code inside the production bundle
```bash
grep -o "next-devtools" .next/static/chunks/ed9f2dc4-*.js | wc -l
# → 27 (expected: 0)

grep -o "dev-overlay" .next/static/chunks/ed9f2dc4-*.js | wc -l
# → 29 (expected: 0)
```

The affected production chunk (`ed9f2dc4-*.js`) ends up ~840–860KB and contains:
- `next-devtools` UI components  
- `dev-overlay` code  
- dev-only CSS and strings like `dev-tools-indicator-menu`  

These should **never** appear in a production bundle.

## Key detail
The issue is triggered only when the dependency graph matches the exact versions from `package-lock.json`.  
Running `npm install` instead of `npm ci` resolves different patch versions, which is why a fresh `create-next-app` does **not** display the bug.

---

### Verified locally:
- Chunk: `ed9f2dc4-36d6f1388b96ed86.js` (≈860KB)  
- `next-devtools`: 27 occurrences  
- `dev-overlay`: 29 occurrences  

---

## Fix verification

I tested this PR's fix against the reproduction:

| Check                         | Before (Next.js 16.1.3) | With this PR |
|------------------------------|--------------------------|---------------|
| `ed9f2dc4-*.js` chunk size   | ~860KB                   | Eliminated    |
| `next-devtools` occurrences  | 27                       | 0             |
| `dev-overlay` occurrences    | 29                       | 0             |

The `NormalModuleReplacementPlugin` correctly intercepts the dev-only modules and replaces them with empty modules, removing ~840KB of dead code from the production bundle.

body: Looks like the issue is caused by the browserslist configuration, as the user-facing deviation from a starter app anyway. Any reason why you have it set like that? Did you mean to have a development time key rather?
author: icyJoseph

body:
Thanks for pointing that out @icyJoseph. 

If Browserslist is indeed what makes this code path reachable, I think the behavior we’re seeing still doesn’t feel right: changing the target shouldn’t make dev-only modules end up in a production bundle.

Even when Browserslist changes how things are compiled, webpack still pulls these dev tools into the dependency graph before dead-code elimination runs. That’s why we see ~860KB of next-devtools/dev overlay code in the client bundle, which no one expects in a prod build.

The NormalModuleReplacementPlugin fix stops those modules from ever getting into the production graph in the first place, regardless of what Browserslist you use.

Either way, the core issue seems to be that dev-only modules are currently reachable in a prod build, and this PR prevents that.

Happy to iterate further!

I am not like dismissing your PR, but the underlying issue is what's important to fix too. Dead code elimination is not working as expected under this specific condition, and while your fix  drops them, the actual impact of the bug is not well understood.

body:
Quick update from my investigation:

- The regression seems to appear around **v15.4.0-canary.113**.
- This lines up with when Browserslist started being passed into SWC’s `env` config.
- With a custom Browserslist, SWC rewrites the ternary `require()` pattern used in `next-devtools/*` in a way that prevents webpack from detecting the dead branch.
- Since webpack resolves `require()` calls before DCE, it ends up including all the dev-only modules in the graph even though they’re inside `process.env.NODE_ENV` guards.
- The later canary.118 change helps in some cases, but doesn’t fully prevent this when certain Browserslist + dependency versions interact.

I’ll continue testing versions around canary.113–118 to pinpoint the exact transformation causing the break.
author: AndreiBalan-dev

body:
Here's the verified root cause after rebuilding the repro multiple times:

- SWC itself is not the issue, the output for default targets vs. custom browserslist is identical *until* env.targets resolves to browser versions SWC doesn’t recognize.

- When browserslist resolves to Chrome/Firefox versions *newer than SWC’s compat data* (e.g., Chrome 142+), SWC applies `async-to-generator` even though those browsers support async/await.

- `fetch-server-response.js` is processed by SWC (it matches Next.js’ include regex), and async-to-generator rewrites:

```
    if ("production" !== "production") {
        await require(...)
    }
``` 

into a generator state machine where the `require()` becomes a separate state transition *outside* the `if` block.

- Webpack’s ConstPlugin can eliminate `require()` inside `if(false) {}`, but it cannot eliminate a `require()` that sits in a generator state machine after an early return. It treats it as reachable and adds the dev-only modules.

This explains the behavior:

- Default targets (Chrome 111) → no async-to-generator → require() stays inside reachable branch → eliminated → 0 KB.
- Future browserslist (Chrome ≥141) → async-to-generator → require() moved outside branch → not eliminated → ~860 KB.

Given this, the NormalModuleReplacementPlugin fix is still the safest approach because it prevents the dev-only modules
from entering the dependency graph regardless of how SWC restructures the code. The real upstream fixes would need to
happen in SWC’s compat data or webpack’s ConstPlugin.

Hey @eliw00d, I appreciate the contribution, but the current maintained stable release is 16.1.

In line with our support policy (https://nextjs.org/support-policy), we won't produce new releases for 16.0 unless there's a critical security release. We only support the latest minor version of any major version.

This is a very straightforward backport of #86653 and #89175, and it seems very safe, so I'll make an exception here and go ahead and merge this into the backport branch, but please know that there are no planned future releases of 16.0.x, and this change will not go out unless it ships alongside a critical security update.

If there are issues discovered with this change during the release of a future security update, this PR may be reverted without notice.

i think this is related to removing the `runRemainingActions` call from the discarded case, runRemainingActions has some special handling for checking if there is a required refresh in the discarded case exactly.
author: lukesandberg

body:
Sure @lukesandberg ! I updated the fix to handle the revalidation case properly.

The new approach:
1. When a discarded action completes with `didRevalidate: true`, we set `actionQueue.needsRefresh = true`
2. We only call `runRemainingActions` when `actionQueue.pending === null` (queue is empty)

This way:
- If another action is still running, we don't corrupt the queue - the running action will pick up `needsRefresh` when it completes
- If the queue is empty, we call `runRemainingActions` which checks `needsRefresh` and triggers the refresh

The "action discarding" tests pass with this change.
author: Suhaib3100

body:
Also added the same `needsRefresh` handling for the error path - if a discarded action fails but had already revalidated data before erroring, we still need to trigger the refresh.

Both success and error paths now:
1. Set `needsRefresh = true` if the discarded action had `didRevalidate: true`  
2. Only call `runRemainingActions` when `pending === null` to avoid queue corruption

body:
Updated the test to improve reliability and fix the CI failure. The core fix in `app-router-instance.ts` is correct – the test just needed timing adjustments.

## Changes Made

**Test Improvements** (`action-queue-transition-deadlock.test.ts`):
- ✅ Increased server action delay from 500ms to 2000ms to ensure the second click reliably happens while the first action is still pending
- ✅ Added `retry()` wrapper for the "other-page" heading check to handle timing issues with page rendering
- ✅ Added explicit verification that the transition completes (`status` returns to `'idle'`) – **this is the key indicator that the deadlock was prevented**
- ✅ Increased retry timeouts (15s → 20s for navigation, added 15s check for transition completion)
- ✅ Changed retry intervals from 1000ms to 500ms for faster, more responsive polling

## Why This Matters

The original bug (#84299) causes transitions to get stuck with `isPending=true` forever when a navigation action is discarded. Your fix resolves the discarded action's promise, allowing React's transition to complete properly. 

The improved test now **explicitly validates** that `isPending` returns to `false` after the navigation completes. If it remained `true`, the deadlock would still be present.

The test should now pass consistently in CI while properly validating the deadlock fix. 🎯

Fixed the CI test failure. The issue was that the heading check was using the default 3000ms timeout, which wasn't enough time on slower CI runners after the 2000ms server action delay + navigation.

## Changes in commit `2427a38355`:
- ✅ Added explicit **10000ms timeout** to the "Other Page" heading check (was using default 3000ms)
- ✅ Increased final transition completion check from **15000ms → 20000ms** to match navigation timeout
- ✅ Added proper retry parameters with consistent 500ms intervals for all checks

All timeouts are now generous enough for CI while still failing fast if there's an actual deadlock. The test should pass consistently now! 🎯

body:
Nice fix!  

Rather than manually building the `@import` string, you could reconstruct an `ImportRule` from the stored attributes and use LightningCSS's built-in `to_css_string()`method. This would be a bit more maintainable if CSS adds new @import attributes in the future. Would you be open to trying that approach?  

This does reveal a slight innacuracy in our modeling of layer names since we flatten them when pulling them off the import rule, so we will want to keep the `Option<Option<LayerName>>` structure so we can model anonymous layers.
author: lukesandberg

body:
> This would be a bit more maintainable if CSS adds new https://github.com/import attributes in the future. Would you be open to trying that approach?

Done, much simpler!

During this, i realize there are no more references to `stringify_js` so I deleted it. It's unnecessary here since LightningCSS handles that with [`serialize_string`](https://github.com/parcel-bundler/lightningcss/blob/master/src/rules/import.rs#L55). 

I wasn't quite sure how to construct the [`Location`](https://github.com/parcel-bundler/lightningcss/blob/master/src/rules/mod.rs#L118) struct for Lightning CSS, there is [`ImportAssetReference.issue_source`](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/2521b8adc73957cf7dfc358bea3c461b04bcfa16/turbopack/crates/turbopack-css/src/references/import.rs#L87) which has Line, Column and Source. But source is an identifier in Turbopack, and in lightning CSS it's expecting a `source_index` which is " The index of the source file within the source map.".  I wonder if `Loc` is even necessary here, considering it's just printing an arbitrary string. 


I added a snapshot test as well, should all of these tests be snapshot tests? I wasn't aware of them when I started but it might be better in the long run.

body:
Looks promising! But I have two concerns about this:

1. Is an instance of a `/ws` route going to stay alive until the user disconnects? If so, what happens if the user stays connected for hours? Even worse, what if there are thousands of users of the app? Are there going to be thousands of instances waiting for users to disconnect?

2. Is this only for browser-to-browser interactions, or would it also be possible to send data from server to browser? For example: Redis pub/sub -> socket

body:
This is a tricky one. 

Right now the docs already instruct users to install `react` and `react-dom` during manual setup, without making that conditional (implicitly made w/ create-next-app). We also call out, both in the installation flow and in the React version handling docs, that the App Router uses the React canary channel internally.

We already explain what needs to be installed and which React version is actually used in App Router.

We added a more prominent note about this in the docs a few months ago (rather recently in terms of App Router lifetime), so much of the confusion being referenced likely predates the current guidance.

The question for me is whether this change helps prevent users from doing something incorrectly, or whether it reflects a concrete issue we are seeing in practice. Right now it reads more like additional background than something that changes user behavior.

That said, if there are specific examples of users misreading the current docs or taking incorrect action as a result, I think it would make sense to iterate with that in mind. For the CVEs, the place to follow guidance from are the Security Advisories published, not the installation page.

I think the PR diff could also be a lot shorter, and I do wonder if the [next CLI](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next) API reference is a better place for a note on this topic. Still not as long as presented here.
author: icyJoseph

body: Thank you for the acknowledgment — I understand that this change may feel overly verbose. I’m happy to shorten the diff and reduce this to a brief note. I can also move it to the Next CLI docs if that’s a better fit and better supports developers, rather than causing confusion.

body: @jjnawaaz how does this PR fix #89430 ?
author: icyJoseph

body:
Hi @icyJoseph, 
The issue body in #89430 appears to be auto-generated and includes an unrelated example component, but the underlying documentation gap is about invoking Server Functions from Client Components outside of form actions.

Today, the docs show examples of calling Server Functions from event handlers, but they don’t explicitly mention that these calls should be wrapped in a React transition (e.g. useTransition) to avoid blocking rendering.

This PR addresses that gap by adding a short clarification in the Event Handlers section of the Updating Data guide, making the expected usage explicit. That clarification is what #89430 is aiming to capture, independent of the pasted example code.
author: jjnawaaz
icyJoseph

body:
@icyJoseph 
Yeah, you’re right that the pasted example in #89430 itself isn’t using Server Functions or Actions.

The reason I linked this PR to that issue is that the issue appears to have been auto-generated or populated with an unrelated example, while still being labeled as a documentation issue in the Next.js repo. Based on that, I interpreted the underlying intent as pointing out a docs gap rather than the specific code sample.

Independently of the example, the current docs do show Server Functions being invoked from event handlers without explicitly mentioning that those calls should be wrapped in a React transition. This PR just adds that missing clarification in the Event Handlers section.

If you think #89430 isn’t the right issue to track this, I’m happy to unlink it or adjust the association - the docs change itself should still be useful on its own.

body: > Hiyo, could you expand a bit more on what happened? > > * [Warn when two versions of React are used alongside facebook/react#2402](https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/2402) -> was it something like this? Hey @icyJoseph! Thanks for referencing the issue. This sounds similar in terms of root-cause since in my case, react@19.0.1 & react-dom@19.0.0 were installed. However, I didn't get any warning, instead the local build failed with a `TypeError` as well as the deployment build: I documented how I encountered this issue [here](https://richard-p6l.com/articles/fixing-prerender-error-in-nextjs-with-multiple-react-versions-installed).
author: p6l-richard

body:
Interesting, I wonder what [`--debug-prerender` ](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#debugging-prerender-errors) would've given you a better stack. 

Also, in App Router, Next.js manages the React version used. That may have been the root issue in your case? That error you got is often seen when one accessed client side APIs (hooks mostly) in a Server Component module graph.
author: icyJoseph

body:
> Interesting, I wonder what [`--debug-prerender` ](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#debugging-prerender-errors) would've given you a better stack.

> Also, in App Router, Next.js manages the React version used. That may have been the root issue in your case? That error you got is often seen when one accessed client side APIs (hooks mostly) in a Server Component module graph. 

Yes, that was precisely the root cause! I don't know the app router manages this, that makes sense, thanks for sharing.

-- 

This PR was meant for users who work in a monorepo setup, where the dep's version is managed via the package as opposed to the app. 

If that sounds valuable, let me know if I can enhance the PR to meet requirements!

body: i don't understand the PR description.  This adjusts the mix of medium and small values, not the size of SST files? or if it does it is indirect from changing the block overheads?
author: lukesandberg

body:
Small values vs medium values is basically a trade-off.

| What? | Inlined | Small value | Medium value | Blob value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compression Size | <= 16kB `MAX_KEY_BLOCK_SIZE`  | <= 4kB (before 64kB) `MAX_SMALL_VALUE_BLOCK_SIZE` | > 1kB (before 64kB) `MAX_SMALL_VALUE_SIZE` | > 64 MB `MAX_MEDIUM_VALUE_SIZE` |
| Compaction | re-compressed | re-compressed | copied compressed | pointer copied |
| Access cost | no extra overhead | uncompress 4kB (before 64kB) | uncompress value size | open separate file, uncompress value size |
| Storage overhead | 0 | 8 + value size / 4kB * 8 | 2 + 8 | 4 + 4 |

### Access cost

The idea of my change was to make accessing small values cheaper: Before every access to a small value needed to decompress 64KiB before it could read the value. Now it only need to decompress 4kiB. Since decompression dominated the access time, this is a big improvement.

### Storage overhead

This change also causes more blocks. The storage overhead of every small value increased from `8 + value size / 64kB * 8` to `8 + value size / 4kB * 8` (so 8 bytes in the key block + 8 bytes in the block table which is distributed to 4KiB of small values). The worse case (max small value of 1024 bytes) would be 8 + 2 = 10 bytes overhead which is 1% of the value. Smaller values have a bigger percentage of overhead, but that was true before:

| size | old                | new                 |
|------|--------------------|---------------------|
| 1    | 0 (inlined)    | 0 (inlined)     |
| 2    | 0 (inlined)    | 0 (inlined)     |
| 4    | 0 (inlined)    | 0 (inlined)     |
| 8    | 0 (inlined)    | 0 (inlined)     |
| 16   | 8.0020 (50.01%)    | 8.0313 (50.20%)     |
| 32   | 8.0039 (25.01%)    | 8.0625 (25.20%)     |
| 64   | 8.0078 (12.51%)    | 8.1250 (12.70%)     |
| 128  | 8.0156 (6.26%)     | 8.2500 (6.45%)      |
| 256  | 8.0313 (3.14%)     | 8.5000 (3.32%)      |
| 512  | 8.0625 (1.57%)     | 9.0000 (1.76%)      |
| 1024 | 8.1250 (0.79%)     | 10.0000 (0.98%)     |
| 2048  | 8.2500 (0.40%)      | 10.0000 (0.49%)     |
| 4096  | 8.5000 (0.21%)      | 10.0000 (0.24%)     |
| 8192  | 9.0000 (0.11%)      | 10.0000 (0.12%)     |
| 16384 | 10.0000 (0.06%)     | 10.0000 (0.06%)     |
| 32768 | 12.0000 (0.04%)     | 10.0000 (0.03%)     |
| 65536 | 16.0000 (0.02%)     | 10.0000 (0.02%)     |
| 131072 | 10.0000 (0.01%)     | 10.0000 (0.01%)     |

So the storage cost difference is very small according to this formula. It's a bit inefficient to use small values that are larger than 1/4 of the small value block size.

But we have to take into account that the 8 bytes in the key block are compressed (tho luke figured out that key blocks are usually not compressed anyway). The 8 bytes in the block table are not compressed. Maybe we should compress the block table and decompress it into memory when we open the SST file?

But a problem we are running into with this increased block size is that we are running into the u16::MAX block limit. I added some code to prevent that, but it makes SST files smaller when hitting the limit. That's probably not what we want here...

### Compression Size

By decreasing the block size (for both small and medium values), we reducing our compression ratio. Compression is more efficient when more data is compressed. For smaller blocks it's recommended to use a compression dictionary. When the compression size is >4kB a compression dictionary isn't really needed anymore as there is enough stuff in the block itself to compress well.

My change caused some (medium value) blocks to be between 1kB and 4kB, which isn't optimal.

I think we could increase the MAX_SMALL_VALUE_SIZE to 4kB to address that.
MAX_SMALL_VALUE_BLOCK_SIZE must be at least 2x of that to avoid very small small value blocks due to fragmentation, but I think we could change it to `MIN_SMALL_VALUE_BLOCK_SIZE` and make it only emit a small value block when we reach that size.
That would cause all small value blocks to be at least that size. In rare cases this could cause the block size to be up to `2 * MIN_SMALL_VALUE_BLOCK_SIZE`.

### Summary

Due to hitting the block count limit and the better compression ratio, I think it makes sense to increase the `MIN_SMALL_VALUE_BLOCK_SIZE` to 8kB, which cuts the block count in half, but double the decompression cost for the access. Sounds acceptable.

This would be the updated table:

|------|--------------------|---------------------|

body:
In production builds, process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS is replaced at compile time by webpack.DefinePlugin with a concrete object literal produced by getImageConfig() in define-env.ts. The Image component therefore never reads from process.env at runtime.

In Jest, SWC runs with globals: null, which disables compile-time env replacement entirely. As a result, process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS remains a real runtime lookup and evaluates to undefined, causing the Image component to fall back and crash on c.deviceSizes.

What this change does-

This change restores production-equivalent behavior in Jest by emulating DefinePlugin at the SWC level:
- jest.ts builds the image config object with the same shape as getImageConfig()
- jest-transformer.ts passes it through the transformer pipeline
- options.ts enables jsc.transform.optimizer.globals.envs and injects __NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS as a JSON-stringified literal
- SWC then replaces process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS at compile time, exactly like webpack.


Why this is safe:
- No runtime image code changes
- No Jest-specific logic in production files
- No process.env mutation
- No new globals or env vars
- Behavior is identical to production builds
- This resolves the issue while keeping the runtime path unchanged.

body:
@styfle The failing Jest image qualities test was caused by the distributed next runtime code not being transformed during Jest execution. Although the image configuration was correctly injected into SWC’s optimizer (to mirror Webpack’s DefinePlugin behavior in production), the next package inside node_modules was excluded from transformation. As a result, the compile-time replacement of process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS never occurred, and the Image component fell back to default qualities.

This change ensures:

- The image configuration from next.config.js is passed through the Jest transformer pipeline.
- SWC injects the config using compile-time optimizer globals (matching production semantics).
- The next package itself is included in Jest’s transpiled packages so its distributed runtime files are transformed.

With these changes, the compile-time replacement now runs inside the shipped next code during tests, and custom image qualities are correctly respected. All related tests pass.

body:
After experimenting with a more targeted approach, I reverted to transpiling the entire next package instead of only specific image-related modules.

The reason is that in production builds, process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS is replaced at compile time via webpack’s DefinePlugin. In the Jest production test environment, however, we are not running the full Next.js build pipeline. Instead, the test installs Next from the packed repo and executes the distributed files.

When we tried limiting the SWC transform to specific next/dist/... image modules, the environment variable replacement was not applied consistently across the full internal dependency graph. Some internal imports inside the next package were still bypassing the transform, which caused process.env.__NEXT_IMAGE_OPTS to remain unresolved at runtime. As a result, the image component fell back to default images.qualities, triggering the warning and failing the test.

Transpiling the entire next package ensures that all internal modules go through the same SWC transformation, making the compile-time replacement behavior consistent with production. While this is broader than the original targeted approach, it is currently the only reliable way to guarantee correct behavior in the Jest production test environment.

If we later introduce a more holistic define-env mechanism for Jest, we could revisit narrowing the scope again. For now, this approach prioritizes correctness and test stability.

## Related work: standalone helpers + wiring PRs

We've created complementary PRs that contribute to this effort:

- **#91580** — Standalone Node.js native stream helpers (`chainNodeStreams`, `createBufferedTransformNode`, `createInlinedDataNodeStream`, `pipeNodeReadableToResponse`, plus 6 head-related transforms: `DplId`, `Metadata`, `Suffix`, `HeadInsertion`, `MoveSuffix`, `RootLayoutValidator`). All callbacks use \`bindSnapshot()\` for correct ALS context propagation — addressing @lubieowoce's feedback on #89859 about the \`runInContext\` pattern.

- **#91583** — Wiring layer that connects the helpers into the render pipeline behind \`experimental.useNodeStreams\`, with a native \`continueFizzStream\` implementation that chains Node.js Transforms instead of WhatWG TransformStreams.

### Why native streams > fast-webstreams

We also benchmarked \`experimental-fast-webstreams\` (#89686) on Node.js v25.7.0 and found it's **-6.7% slower** on complex routes (10 nested layouts). Node 25's native WhatWG streams have improved enough that the fast-webstreams interop layer adds overhead. Native Node.js streams bypass the WhatWG API entirely, which is the better long-term path.

### Additional perf PRs (benchmarked +11.5% on web streams path)

We also have 14 micro-optimization PRs (#91559-#91577) targeting non-stream hotspots (structuredClone elimination in metadata resolution at 914ms, tracer early exit, pre-compiled regex, O(1) header lookups, etc.) that deliver +11.5% throughput independently of the stream implementation.

body:
We ran into a similar issue on a project using next@16.2.4 with Turbopack.

In the dev build, styles with the same specificity are chunked in one order, while in production they are chunked in a different order and end up overriding each other. We do not have any specific build rules for SCSS modules.

We are really looking forward to a fix soon 🫶

body:
really cool thanks @sokra

in the meantime we moved away from this.importModule to worker based solution which runs .ts files directly from node.js:

https://github.com/DigitecGalaxus/next-yak/issues/456

our biggest issue is that we can't cache per compilation because there is no this._compilation api (we opened a pr for that but it was ignored) and there is no way to know which files changed for the current compilation
author: jantimon

body:
I see. I think we probably don't want to give you access to mtimes (risky due to race conditions) or changed files (not pure).

But we could give you an API that reads the hash of a file (and adds the file as dependency).

You can feed the hashes into the cache system to find the changed files.

Note that a loader should be a pure function without (visible) state. That's very important for caching and persisting.

body:
A couple of things here. The guide, AFAIK, was meant to be minimal, foundational if you will, covering routing and dictionary loading. We do list a number of libraries and examples that extend the guide.

If I understand correctly, you want to showcase interpolation, but then, the question is, why not add pluralization, nested key access, and expand into ICU Message Format... suddenly the guide is a mini library for i18n.

Each of the libraries and references added in the guide, develops these concepts in full detail, for instance next-intl does that here: https://next-intl.dev/docs/usage/translations

I say this, because, the PR is also making an assumption about the `{{placeholder}}` convention. It is never explained nor put to use, nor any potential edge cases, or what to do if the value for a placeholder is not passed, etc... it is not a trivial topic. 

Also, the guide is using nested objects for scoping, like `{products: { cart: "" }}`, but the suggested implementation would not be able to handle those right?

I think we should close the PR as it is right now. Let's develop the issue you opened first.

body:
## Benchmark on Node.js v25.7.0

I tested this on Node.js v25.7.0 (the version Next.js uses in production with `NODE_OPTIONS="--import tsx"`) and the results are different from the v22 benchmarks:

### Setup
- `patchGlobalWebStreams()` called in a wrapper before `minimal-server.js` loads
- `experimental-fast-webstreams@0.0.19`
- Same machine, `autocannon` with warmup

### Results

| Route | Native WhatWG | fast-webstreams | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simple `/rsc` (c=1) | 5,131 req/s | 5,220 req/s | +1.7% |
| Simple `/rsc` (c=100) | 6,105 req/s | 6,067 req/s | -0.6% |
| **Deep 10-layout** (c=50) | **624 req/s** | **582 req/s** | **-6.7%** |

### Analysis

On Node.js v25, native WhatWG streams have improved significantly compared to v22. The fast-webstreams interop layer (which wraps Node.js streams behind the WhatWG API) now adds overhead for complex workloads:

- The deep route (10 nested layouts, 10 dynamic params, `headers()` + `cookies()` calls) creates 6-8 TransformStreams per request. The interop cost between fast-webstreams' internal Node.js streams and the WhatWG-compatible API compounds across these chained transforms.
- For simple routes, the difference is within noise (~1%).

### Recommendation

For Node.js v25+, **native Node.js streams** (PRs #91580, #91583, #89566) are the better path. They bypass the WhatWG API entirely rather than trying to make it faster, avoiding both the native WhatWG overhead and the fast-webstreams interop overhead.

The node-streams rewrite (#89566) showed +42-46% throughput even on v22 — native piping avoids the per-chunk Promise overhead that both native WhatWG and fast-webstreams still incur.

As part of the CVE's disclosed, we decided to temporarily take back the recommendation. It is still available in our v15 docs. 

The path forward for now is to reintroduce a note about Remote MDX, showing patterns secure by default, even if it introduces friction for developers.
author: icyJoseph

body:
Thank you for your answer. The "Remote MDX" section previously featured the community-driven [next-mdx-remote-client](https://github.com/ipikuka/next-mdx-remote-client) package. To proactively address and minimize the impact of the disclosed CVEs, a specialized utility called [remark-mdx-remove-expressions](https://github.com/ipikuka/remark-mdx-remove-expressions) has been developed.

This plugin is specifically designed to be integrated into workflows like `next-mdx-remote-client` to strip potentially malicious logic from remote content. There is an active discussion regarding this security strategy in [next-mdx-remote-client/issues/18](https://github.com/ipikuka/next-mdx-remote-client/issues/18).

The recommendation for scenarios where the developer does not have full control over the remote MDX source is to utilize **`remark-mdx-remove-expressions`** with the **`{ onlyDangerousExpressions: true }`** option. This provides a "secure by default" layer by neutralizing executable code while preserving the descriptive power of MDX.

I would highly appreciate it **if you could review** the insights shared in [this issue](https://github.com/ipikuka/next-mdx-remote-client/issues/18), as it might provide the secure pattern needed to reintroduce the Remote MDX documentation without compromising user safety.

Basically, rework `Deep Dive: How do you transform markdown into HTML?`

body:
Thanks for the PR

I do believe this behavior is backed by this e2e:

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/c76b0fe2a0bcf971ccc7008ee201244df872f52d/test/e2e/app-dir/hooks/hooks.test.ts#L148-L150

Where, pathnames like, `/hooks/use-selected-layout-segment/first/slug2/second/a/b`, are expected to end up with a `a/b` entry.

I think the bulletpoints are a good idea, they should stay, but we need to reinforce this gotcha by adding an entry to the `Returns` tables, like so, adding a small section after the existing tables:

For `use-selected-layout-segment.mdx`

```
For catch-all routes (`[...slug]`), the returned segment contains all matched path segments joined as a single string:

| Layout                    | Visited URL       | Returned Segment |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| `app/blog/layout.js`      | `/blog/a/b/c`     | `'a/b/c'`        |

```

For `use-selected-layout-segments.mdx`

```
For catch-all routes (`[...slug]`), all matched path segments are returned as a single joined string within the array:

| Layout                    | Visited URL       | Returned Segments    |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- | -------------------- |
| `app/layout.js`           | `/blog/a/b/c`     | `['blog', 'a/b/c']`  |
| `app/blog/layout.js`      | `/blog/a/b/c`     | `['a/b/c']`          |
```

> The linear regression stuff is interesting but for the purposes of the test can’t you just check if it exceeds some constant?

Yeah, fair point, it is a bit more than strictly needed. The reason I went with it is noise resistance: a simple "last minus first" check puts all its weight on two measurements, so if either fluctuates (GC timing, etc.) it can be misleading. The regression spreads that across all the data points, which felt worth the few extra lines.

body: > I would adjust the PR title. This is way more invasive than just owner stacks. How about "Build with dev runtimes when `--debug-prerender` is set"? > How does `--debug-prerender` interact with `next start` e.g. do we consider the built app runnable or do we not guarantee that it works? This generally works, I'm not sure about guarantees though. I'd still consider it an edge case, as `next build --debug-prerender` is mostly meant for CLI-focused debugging, not browser-focused debugging. For that, we still recommend using `next dev`. We do have a couple of tests in `cache-components-errors.test.ts` that don't fail the build and use `next start` for some runtime assertions. They cover testing that `next start` generally works. We're also using the dev bundles for the browser in that case. But no Next.js dev server features are enabled (e.g. React can't fetch source maps for server components via `findSourceMapURL`).

body:
Ok, I think we'll do like this, 🙏 - I think there's a slightly bigger problem here:

1. Keep the table change
2. Let's add a bullet point to all three properties (~ line 98, 112, 123 approx)

- If omitted, defaults to `"default"` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see /docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes)

- If omitted, defaults to the default profile's revalidate value (15 minutes). 

- If omitted, defaults to the default profile's expire value (never expires).

3. Instead of `If you omit `expire`, the cache will never expire, similar to the `default` profile.`, add this right after the snippet

```
> **Good to know**: Any omitted properties in a custom profile inherit from the `default` profile.
```

Maybe should also say: This also applies to inline profile objects passed directly to `cacheLife()`.

4. Way later at line 570-ish

```js
  cacheLife({
    // Ensure post.revalidateSeconds is a number in seconds
    // stale and expire inherit from 'default' profile
    revalidate: post.revalidateSeconds ?? 3600,
  })
```

Let's reinforce this idea. Make sure the highlight is still correct

---

Thanks for the PR!
author: icyJoseph

body:
> I had a bit of back and fort here, because 1 year expire time, in practical terms is negligible - aka, I chose to focus on intent (given that this effectively means, no visits at all, for one 1 year) Did you have an actual problem at runtime? Did you see max and default as equals in that dimension?

No, I didn't encounter an actual runtime issue — this came from reading the source code to understand the cacheLife API.

The main thing that caught my attention was that the docs listed both default and max as "1 year" for expire, which made them appear identical in that dimension. But looking at the code, default uses INFINITE_CACHE while max uses 60*60*24*365, so they're intentionally different values. I completely agree that the practical difference is negligible, but I thought aligning the docs with the actual code would help avoid confusion for anyone reading both.

That said, the bigger motivation was that the docs didn't mention what happens when expire is omitted entirely — which I think is useful for users defining custom or inline profiles.

Thank you for the detailed feedback — I'll update the PR accordingly!

body: Hey @unstubbable — saw your fix in #93294, looks like we're both tackling #54077. This PR is more of a downstream safety net (fallback in `change()` when `resolvedAs` doesn't match the route pattern). Would love your eyes on it if you get a chance!
author: VrajKD

body:
Hey @VrajKD, I tried your fixture against the latest canary and it passes in all three modes I tested (turbopack-prod, webpack-prod, turbopack-dev) without any change to `router.ts`. Same result with the original `ferenckv/next-router-bug` setup. Looks like #54077 got fixed by something unrelated in the years since, so I dropped the "fixes #54077" line from my PR description since it was misleading.

#93294 isn't really overlapping with this. It's for a different code path. The scenario I hit needs basePath + a rewrite + middleware + a catch-all dynamic route, and the corruption is upstream in `getMiddlewareData()`, not in the place where you're adding the fallback. With a catch-all, `routeInfo.resolvedAs` ends up holding the data URL, the catch-all regex matches the multi-segment input, and `router.query.<param>` gets overwritten with the data-URL segments. Single-segment dynamic routes don't show it because their regex rejects the multi-segment input.

Mind double-checking whether your fixture still fails for you on canary? If it doesn't, the fallback here might not be load-bearing anymore.
author: unstubbable
